newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Ciller seen safe from corruption charges.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller seen safe from corruption charges.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led governing coalition is set to emerge strengthened from a corruption tangle on Wednesday but the powerful military is waiting in the wings to halt any slide from official secularism.
MPs are to vote later in the day on whether to send Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller to the Supreme Court on the last of three corruption charges.
Conservative Ciller, who is also the foreign minister, comfortably won two similar votes on Tuesday and deputies said she was likely to weather the latest ballot.
The opposition's best showing on Tuesday was 257 votes, well short of the 276 needed to impeach Ciller, prime minister from 1993-96.
A censure motion against Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, set for consideration on February 25, is likewise expected to go the government's way.
Ciller dismissed opposition charges of rifts in her alliance with Erbakan. "This government will continue," she told a meeting of her True Path Party ahead of the vote.
Stocks in Istanbul rose 1.63 percent in morning trading on positive political hopes after Tuesday's votes.
Many MPs from Erbakan's Welfare Party who had backed graft accusations against Ciller when they were in opposition last year voted for her this time, in an about-turn to protect coalition unity.
Erbakan's administration has begun to show cracks recently despite successful joint efforts on privatisation.
Several True Path ministers have criticised plans by Erbakan to increase the profile of Islam in public life.
The proposals are mild but they have sparked wide public debate on Turkey's 70-year-old secularist system and rumours of military intervention against the Islamists.

"Let's not politicise secularism and religion," Ciller said in a call for calm. "We are not going to become a world power by spending our time asking ourselves if we are going to become another Algeria," she said.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algerian violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
The Sabah newspaper said this week that the head of Turkey's armed forces, General Ismail Hakki Karadayi, would warn Erbakan not to ditch secularism when they talked at a security meeting next week.

"The army is not happy," commentator and military expert Mehmet Ali Birand told Reuters. But he said Erbakan would assure the generals that he has no intention of turning NATO member Turkey into an Islamic state.
"(The meeting) will give us a few months breathing space and then we will start over again," Birand said. Karadayi is to visit Israel this month, a foreign ministry spokesman said.
Pro-Western Ciller had previously vowed not to go into coalition with the Islamists but she dropped her strong opposition to Erbakan under a wave of corruption charges.
